problems.body: A tightrope stops at both towers. How many endpoints does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: 0 endpoints describes a line, which never stops. This tightrope stops at both towers: 2 endpoints.
1 endpoint describes a ray, which keeps going one way. This tightrope stops at BOTH ends: 2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count how many definite stopping points the tightrope has.

explanationVariants: Two towers, two endpoints — a line segment.
Stopping at both ends means 2 endpoints.

problems.body: A sunbeam starts at the sun and travels forever in one direction. What geometric term fits best?

options.label: Ray
options.feedback: One endpoint (the sun), traveling one direction forever — a ray.

options.label: Line segment
options.feedback: A segment has TWO endpoints. The sunbeam only starts at the sun and keeps going — a ray.

options.label: Line
options.feedback: A line has NO endpoints and goes both ways. The sunbeam clearly starts at the sun — a ray.

explanationVariants: One endpoint, one direction — a ray.
The sun marks the single starting point.

problems.body: An angle is named XYZ. Which point is the vertex?

options.label: X
options.feedback: X is the first letter, a point on one ray. The vertex is the MIDDLE letter: Y.

options.label: Y
options.feedback: The vertex is always the middle letter: Y.

options.label: Z
options.feedback: Z is the last letter, a point on the other ray. The vertex is the MIDDLE letter: Y.

hints: The vertex is always the middle letter.
explanationVariants: The middle letter of any three-letter angle name is the vertex: Y.
X and Z sit on the rays; Y is where they meet.

problems.body: Two rays share a starting point at point B, spreading toward points A and C. What is point B called?

options.label: The vertex
options.feedback: The shared starting point of two rays is always the vertex.

options.label: A side
options.feedback: The SIDES are the two rays themselves. B, where they meet, is the vertex.

options.label: A line segment
options.feedback: B is a single point, not a segment. It's the vertex where the two rays meet.

hints: B is where the two rays meet.
That shared point has a name.
explanationVariants: The shared point of two rays is the vertex.
B is the vertex; A and C sit on the rays.

problems.body: Three rays share one vertex. How many different angles do these three rays form?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 only counts the outer angle. Two more hide between the individual pairs of rays: 3 total.
2 misses one pair. Every possible pair of the 3 rays forms its own angle: 3 total.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count every possible pair among the 3 rays.

hints: Every pair of rays forms its own angle.
explanationVariants: 3 rays create 3 distinct pairs, so 3 angles.
Count every combination of two rays: 3.

problems.body: Five rays share one vertex. How many different angles do these five rays form?

commonErrors.feedback: 5 just counts the rays themselves, not the angles between them. Every PAIR of the 5 rays forms its own angle: 10 total.
4 undercounts significantly. Every possible pair among 5 rays gives 10 angles.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count every possible pair among the 5 rays.

hints: Every pair of rays forms its own angle.
explanationVariants: 5 rays create 10 distinct pairs, so 10 angles.
Count every combination of two rays: 10.

problems.body: Two lines stay exactly the same distance apart forever, never touching. What are they called?

options.label: Parallel
options.feedback: Constant distance and never touching is exactly the definition of parallel.

options.label: Perpendicular
options.feedback: Perpendicular lines CROSS at a right angle. These lines never cross at all — parallel.

options.label: Intersecting
options.feedback: Intersecting lines meet at a point. Lines that never touch are parallel.

explanationVariants: Never touching, constant distance — parallel.
The definition matches parallel exactly.

problems.body: A fence's two rails always stay the same distance apart. Are they parallel?

options.label: Yes
options.feedback: Constant distance apart, never crossing — parallel.

options.label: Only if the fence is very long
options.feedback: Length isn't the test — constant distance is, and that's true here regardless of length.

options.label: No
options.feedback: Constant distance apart with no crossing is exactly the parallel definition — these rails ARE parallel.

explanationVariants: Constant spacing, no crossing — parallel.
The rails meet the parallel test exactly.

problems.body: Two lines cross, forming a perfect right angle. What are they called?

options.label: Perpendicular
options.feedback: Crossing at exactly 90° is the definition of perpendicular.

options.label: Parallel
options.feedback: Parallel lines NEVER cross. These lines DO cross, at a right angle — perpendicular.

options.label: Rays
options.feedback: A ray is about one endpoint and direction, not two crossing lines. A 90° crossing is perpendicular.

explanationVariants: A right-angle crossing is perpendicular.
90° crossings define perpendicular lines.

problems.body: Two lines cross at 89°. Are they perpendicular?

options.label: No — perpendicular requires exactly 90°
options.feedback: 89° is close, but perpendicular means EXACTLY 90° — one degree off disqualifies it.

options.label: Yes — 89° is basically 90°
options.feedback: Perpendicular has no 'basically' — it means exactly 90°. At 89°, these lines are just crossing.

options.label: Yes, since it's so close
options.feedback: Closeness doesn't count — perpendicular requires exactly 90°, and 89 isn't 90.

explanationVariants: 89° falls short of the exact 90° needed.
Only exactly 90° counts as perpendicular.

problems.body: A plus sign's (+) two strokes cross at exactly 90°. What is this relationship called?

options.label: Perpendicular
options.feedback: A 90° crossing is perpendicular.

options.label: Parallel
options.feedback: Parallel lines never cross at all. These clearly cross at 90° — perpendicular.

options.label: Just an estimate
options.feedback: A plus sign's crossing is precisely 90°, not an estimate — perpendicular.

explanationVariants: A plus sign's exact right-angle crossing is perpendicular.
90° is the perpendicular benchmark.

problems.body: How many pairs of PARALLEL sides does a rectangle have?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 counts every side, not just the parallel PAIRS. Only opposite sides are parallel: top-bottom and left-right — 2 pairs.
1 undercounts — a rectangle has TWO pairs of opposite sides, both parallel.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count only the OPPOSITE side pairs, which never meet.

hints: A rectangle has 2 pairs of opposite sides.
explanationVariants: Top-bottom and left-right — 2 parallel pairs.
Every rectangle has exactly 2 parallel pairs.

problems.body: A tic-tac-toe grid has 2 horizontal lines and 2 vertical lines. How many perpendicular crossing PAIRS does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: 2 only counts one line from each direction. Each of the 2 horizontal lines crosses EACH of the 2 vertical lines: 2×2=4.
8 overcounts. There are only 2 horizontal and 2 vertical lines — 2×2=4 crossing pairs.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Multiply the number of horizontal lines by the number of vertical lines.

explanationVariants: 2×2=4 perpendicular crossing pairs.
Every horizontal-vertical combination is one pair.

problems.body: A window has a plus-shaped divider: 3 vertical lines and 3 horizontal lines total. How many perpendicular crossing PAIRS does it create?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 undercounts. There are 3 verticals AND 3 horizontals — every vertical crosses every horizontal: 3×3=9.
3 only counts one direction. Multiply the verticals by the horizontals: 3×3=9.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Multiply the number of vertical lines by the number of horizontal lines.

explanationVariants: 3×3=9 perpendicular crossing pairs.
Every vertical-horizontal combination is one pair.

problems.body: A triangle has angles 60°, 60°, and 60°. What type of triangle is it?

options.label: Acute
options.feedback: Every angle is under 90° — acute.

options.label: Right
options.feedback: Right needs exactly one angle at 90°. None of these reach it — acute.

options.label: Obtuse
options.feedback: Obtuse needs an angle over 90°. All three here are only 60° — acute.

explanationVariants: The largest angle, 60°, is under 90° — acute.
All three equal angles stay under the right-angle benchmark.

problems.body: A triangle has angles 90°, 45°, and 45°. What type of triangle is it?

options.label: Right
options.feedback: One angle is exactly 90° — right.

options.label: Acute
options.feedback: Acute needs every angle under 90°. One angle here is exactly 90° — right, not acute.

options.label: Obtuse
options.feedback: Obtuse needs an angle over 90°. The largest here is exactly 90° — right, not obtuse.

explanationVariants: The largest angle, exactly 90°, makes this a right triangle.
One angle at exactly 90° is the right-triangle signal.

problems.body: A triangle has angles 100°, 40°, and 40°. What type of triangle is it?

options.label: Obtuse
options.feedback: The largest angle, 100°, is over 90° — obtuse.

options.label: Acute
options.feedback: Acute needs every angle under 90°. 100° is well past that — obtuse.

options.label: Right
options.feedback: Right needs an angle at exactly 90°. None of these is 90° — the largest, 100°, makes it obtuse.

explanationVariants: The largest angle, 100°, exceeds 90° — obtuse.
One angle past the right-angle benchmark makes it obtuse.

problems.body: A triangle has two angles: 50° and 60°. What is the third angle?

commonErrors.feedback: 110 is just the sum of the two known angles — not the missing one yet. Subtract it from 180: 70.
10 subtracts one known angle from the other instead of using the 180° total. Add 50+60=110, then subtract from 180: 70.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Add the two known angles, then subtract that total from 180.

explanationVariants: 50+60=110; the third angle is 180−110=70.
Every triangle's three angles total 180°.

problems.body: A right triangle has a 90° angle and a 35° angle. What is the third angle?

commonErrors.feedback: 125 is just the sum of the two known angles — not the missing one yet. Subtract it from 180: 55.
90 just repeats one of the known angles. The three angles must total 180: 180−(90+35)=55.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Add 90 and 35, then subtract that total from 180.

explanationVariants: 90+35=125; the third angle is 180−125=55.
Even a right triangle's angles still total 180°.

problems.body: An obtuse triangle has angles 120° and 35°. What is the third angle?

commonErrors.feedback: 155 is just the sum of the two known angles — not the missing one yet. Subtract it from 180: 25.
60 doesn't match this pair. Add 120+35=155, then subtract from 180: 25.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Add 120 and 35, then subtract that total from 180.

explanationVariants: 120+35=155; the third angle is 180−155=25.
Every triangle type still totals 180°.

problems.body: A quadrilateral has three angles of exactly 90° and one angle of 85°. Is it a true rectangle?

options.label: No — the 85° angle fails the all-four-90° rule
options.feedback: Even one corner short of exactly 90° means this fails the rectangle's entry rule.

options.label: Yes — three out of four is close enough
options.feedback: The rectangle rule allows no exceptions. One angle at 85° means this isn't a true rectangle.

options.label: Yes — 85° is basically 90°
options.feedback: The entry rule is exact, not approximate. 85° falls short of 90°.

hints: A rectangle needs ALL FOUR angles at 90°.
explanationVariants: 85° fails the all-four-90° rectangle rule.
Even one exception disqualifies it from the rectangle club.

problems.body: Three angles of a quadrilateral are each exactly 90°. What must the fourth angle be?

commonErrors.feedback: 270 is just the sum of the three knowns (90+90+90). A quadrilateral's angles total 360°: 360−270=90.
0 isn't a valid angle for a real quadrilateral. The fourth angle must be 360−270=90.

widget.fallbackFeedback: A quadrilateral's four angles total 360°. Subtract the three knowns from 360.

explanationVariants: Three 90° angles force the fourth to be 90° too, since 360−270=90.
This is why exactly three right angles is impossible — the fourth always follows.

problems.body: A four-sided shape has no angles that measure exactly 90°. Is it still a valid quadrilateral?

options.label: Yes — quadrilateral only requires 4 sides
options.feedback: Being a quadrilateral just means having 4 sides. Right angles are the separate rectangle rule.

options.label: No — every quadrilateral needs at least one right angle
options.feedback: There's no such requirement. A quadrilateral just needs 4 sides.

options.label: No — it must be some other shape entirely
options.feedback: A 4-sided shape is a quadrilateral regardless of its angles.

hints: Right angles are a separate, stricter rule.
explanationVariants: 4 sides alone makes it a quadrilateral — no angle requirement.
Right angles matter only for the rectangle club specifically.

problems.body: Folding a square straight down the middle: do the two halves match exactly?

options.label: Yes
options.feedback: Both halves are identical rectangles — a perfect match.

options.label: No
options.feedback: A square folded down the middle produces two identical halves — they DO match.

options.label: Only if it's folded diagonally
options.feedback: Straight down the middle also works for a square — both fold directions produce matches.

explanationVariants: A square's straight-down-the-middle fold produces matching halves.
This fold line is a genuine line of symmetry.

problems.body: A scalene triangle (no two sides equal), folded any way: do the halves ever match?

options.label: No
options.feedback: With no matching sides or angles anywhere, no fold produces matching halves.

options.label: Yes, if folded through the center
options.feedback: Even a center fold won't help — the sides are all different lengths, so no fold can match them.

options.label: Yes, every triangle has a line of symmetry
options.feedback: Not every triangle does. A scalene triangle, with all different sides, has zero lines of symmetry.

hints: No fold can match unequal sides.
explanationVariants: A scalene triangle has zero lines of symmetry.
With no matching sides anywhere, no fold succeeds.

problems.body: A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides. How many lines of symmetry does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 would be half the sides. For a REGULAR shape, the symmetry count matches the full side count: 6.
12 doubles the side count. For a regular shape, symmetry lines equal the side count exactly: 6.

widget.fallbackFeedback: For a regular shape, count the sides — that's also the symmetry-line count.

explanationVariants: 6 equal sides give 6 lines of symmetry.
The regular-shape pattern holds here too.

problems.body: A rectangle (not a square) has unequal sides. How many lines of symmetry does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 would be right for a SQUARE, where all sides are equal. This rectangle's unequal sides mean its diagonals don't work — only 2.
0 undercounts — the horizontal and vertical center lines both still produce a match. That's 2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Only the horizontal and vertical center lines work for a non-square rectangle.

hints: Only the center lines work here.
Not the diagonals — sides are unequal.
explanationVariants: A non-square rectangle has exactly 2 lines of symmetry.
Unequal sides rule out the diagonals as symmetry lines.

problems.body: A regular octagon has 8 equal sides. How many lines of symmetry does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 would be half the sides. For a REGULAR shape, the symmetry count matches the full side count: 8.
16 doubles the side count. For a regular shape, symmetry lines equal the side count exactly: 8.

widget.fallbackFeedback: For a regular shape, count the sides — that's also the symmetry-line count.

explanationVariants: 8 equal sides give 8 lines of symmetry.
A stop sign's shape follows this same pattern.

problems.body: Does the block capital letter H have BOTH a vertical and a horizontal line of symmetry?

options.label: Yes
options.feedback: H matches left-right AND top-bottom — both.

options.label: Only vertical
options.feedback: H's top and bottom halves also match when folded horizontally — it has both.

options.label: Only horizontal
options.feedback: H's left and right halves also match when folded vertically — it has both.

hints: Fold H down the middle — matches.
Fold H across the middle — also matches.
explanationVariants: H has both vertical and horizontal symmetry.
Both fold directions produce a match for H.

problems.body: The letter N looks the same when spun 180°. Does N have a LINE of symmetry (a fold that matches, not a spin)?

options.label: No — that's rotational symmetry, a different idea from folding
options.feedback: Looking the same after a spin is rotational symmetry. No fold line makes N's two halves match.

options.label: Yes — looking the same after spinning counts
options.feedback: Spinning and folding test different things. N passes the spin test but fails the fold test — no line of symmetry.

options.label: Yes, through its diagonal stroke
options.feedback: Folding along N's diagonal doesn't make the two halves mirror each other — that's still the spin property, not a fold match.

hints: Spinning and folding are different tests.
N passes the spin test, not the fold test.
explanationVariants: N has rotational symmetry, but no line of symmetry.
Spin-matching and fold-matching are separate properties.
